abstract: The electrochemical reduction of CO2 into C2+ products is a promising route to store renewable electricity in the form of chemical energy. The current barrier to this technique is the low efficiency of C-C coupling through dimerization of adsorbed *CO or coupling of *CO with its hydrogenated derivatives over the Cu catalyst. Tandem catalysts, which integrate Cu with another CO-generation catalyst (e.g., ZnO), can enhance the C-C coupling kinetics by increasing the local concentration of the key intermediate of CO. However, the degree of enhancement is strongly dependent on the spatial manipulation of supplementary CO transport. Herein, inspired by the reactant species concentration profile in a plug flow reactor, Cu/ZnO tandem electrodes are designed by spatially adding a ZnO catalyst layer on top of the Cu catalyst layer, in which the ZnO catalyst layer fed CO concentration progressively decreases over the Cu catalyst layer. Such a spatial management of CO transport dramatically increases the CO utilization efficiency, leading to an enhancement of Faradaic efficiency and partial current density of C2+ products by 1.2 and 3.4 times, respectively, compared to the bare Cu electrode, while by 1.3 and 1.8 times, respectively, compared to the Cu&ZnO mixed electrode.

sections.text:
1 Enhance CO2-to-C2+ products yield through spatial management of CO transport in Cu/ZnO tandem electrodes
Keywords: Cu/ZnO, tandem reaction, CO transport, C2+ products, ethylene
2

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The electrochemical upgrading of CO2 into carbon-based chemicals and fuels provides a mean to close the anthropogenic carbon cycle and store excess renewable electricity in chemical energy. Among the C2-C3 products, ethylene (C2H4) is the two-carbon product of particular interest due to its both high market demand and price as a chemical feedstock. Copper (Cu) is a well-known electrocatalyst capable of catalyzing the formation of multicarbon (C2+) products due to its unique d-band center.[1, 2] So far, many strategies at the catalyst level such as control over morphology, facets, oxidation state, dopants, and strain have been explored in order to improve the activity and selectivity towards C2+ products on Cu based catalysts.[3-10] However, the overpotential and selectivity of Cu towards C2+ products formation are limited by a trade-off between high CO production rate and high CO-CO coupling rate, which is imposed by linear scaling relations of intermediates adsorption energy and the Brønsted–Evans–Polanyi (BEP) linear correlations linking the activation energy with binding energies of intermediates[11, 12]. The tandem reaction is a promising strategy to break the linear scaling relations since the overall CO2 electro-reduction is conducted on two distinct, segregated active sites: the CO2 is firstly converted to CO on CO-selective sites (e.g., Zn, Ag, and Au), followed by cascade dimerization and hydrogenation reaction of CO on C2+ products-selective sites (e.g., Cu).[13-18] Tandem catalysts involving two segregated active sites, such as core-shell Cu@ZnO and Ag-Cu dimers, have shown an enhancement of the Faradaic efficiency (FE) and production rate of C2+ products over alloy,[16] [17] although such improvement may partly originate from the alternation of strain and electronic structure over Cu. In contarts, many reports have also shown that the Cu-based bimetallic metals exhibited even lower FE of C2+ products than the compositional element, [13, 15, 16, 19-22] due largely to the inefficient utilization of CO intermediate. The key to cascade process of CO2 electro-reduction is to maximize the CO-CO coupling reaction rate via increasing the local CO concentration at the Cu surface because the reaction order n of CO-CO coupling is positive with respect to CO (Figure S1).[14, 18] Therefore, the temporal and spatial profile of the local CO concentration at the electrode level, which is determined by the spatial arrangement and mass loading of respective catalysts in the catalyst layer, is key to enhance the production efficiency and yield of C2+ products simultaneously. In the case of the electrodes made from tandem catalysts, the local CO concentration throughout the catalyst layer, analogous to that in a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR), is uniform but relatively lower than that in a plug flow reactor (PFR). That is because the supplementary CO comes locally from the CO-generation catalytic sites, resulting in a low utilization efficiency of CO for further coupling and/or reduction. This explains an increase of the FE of CO in various extents on the tandem catalyst-made electrodes compared with the electrodes fabricated from the bare Cu catalyst.[13, 15, 16, 18, 20, 23] From the perspective of chemical reaction engineering, a PFR is preferred over a CSTR in order to promote the CO-CO coupling rate to yield C2+ products (Figure S2). Herein, instead of the extensive research on tandem catalysts, we designed layer-by-layer
3 tandem electrodes, which can efficiently utilize the CO in a way analogous to the PFR along the catalyst layer thickness. As a proof-of-concept, the commercial ZnO and Cu nanoparticles were used as the CO- and C2+-selective catalysts, respectively. The two-layer Cu/ZnO tandem electrode exhibits 1.8 times increase in the production rate of C2+ products compared to the CSTR equivalent one-layer electrode composed of physically mixed Cu and ZnO nanoparticles (referred to Cu&ZnO mixed electrode). Moreover, Cu/ZnO tandem electrodes direct the tandem catalysis process with simultaneously high production efficiency and rate of C2+ products superior to those for the bare Cu electrode and previous Cu and Zn based bimetallic tandem catalysts.

sections.heading: 2.1 Preparation of the bare Cu electrode.
sections.text: The bare Cu electrode was prepared by a typical air brush method. Initially, a Cu catalyst ink was prepared by mixing Cu nanoparticles (4.0 mg, Sigma), Nafion (10.0 μl), iso-propanol (800.0 μl), and H2O (800.0 μl) together, and then sonicated for 20 min. After that, this catalyst ink was uniformly air-brushed onto a carbon paper (4.0 cm2, Sigracet GDL 34BC) and then dried by a vacuum oven for 1 h at 130 oC. This bare Cu electrode is named as Cu1.0 to represent the Cu loading of 1.0 mg cm-2.

sections.heading: 2.2 Preparation of the Cu/ZnO tandem electrodes.
sections.text: The tandem electrodes were prepared by sequential air brush method. The ZnO (Sigma) catalyst ink was prepared by the same way as that of Cu ink. While the Cu loading was kept at 1.0 mg cm-2, five loadings for ZnO catalyst layer were used: 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, and 0.30 mg cm-2. The ZnO catalyst ink was air-brushed onto the bare Cu electrode according to the designed loading. After the air-brush, the electrodes were dried by vacuum oven for 1 h at 130 oC. These five tandem electrodes with different ratios are named as Cu1.0/ZnO0.05, Cu1.0/ZnO0.10, Cu1.0/ZnO0.15, Cu1.0/ZnO0.20 and Cu1.0/ZnO0.30. The number following the catalyst reflects the loading.

sections.heading: 2.3 Preparation of the Cu/Pt/ZnO tandem electrodes.
sections.text: The three-layer Cu/Pt/ZnO electrodes were prepared by the sequential air brush as well. The Cu catalyst ink was prepared by the same way as that of bare Cu electrode. The ZnO catalyst ink was the same as that of Cu1.0/ZnO0.15 electrode. The Pt/C (Alfa Aesar) catalyst inks were made by the same way as that of the Cu catalyst ink while the weight of Pt/C is 1.0 mg. The amount of Nafion was reduced proportionally as the ratio of Pt/C to Cu, while the amount of iso-propanol and H2O were both set to be 2.0 ml. Then, the Cu/Pt/ZnO tandem electrodes were prepared by spraying these three catalyst inks in a sequence of Cu, Pt/C and ZnO, while the amount of Pt/C catalyst ink was set to be 1.60 ml and 160.0 ul for the Cu : Pt/C ratio of 1.0 : 0.10 and 1.0 : 0.01, respectively. After the air-brush, the electrodes were dried by a vacuum oven for 1 h at 130 oC. These two Cu/Pt/ZnO tandem electrodes are named of Cu1.0/Pt0.01/ZnO0.15 and Cu1.0/Pt0.10/ZnO0.15, respectively.

sections.heading: 2.4 Regular CO2 electro-reduction reaction.
sections.text:
The CO2 electro-reduction reaction was conducted in a customized flow cell. The CO2
4 stream of 15.00 sccm was controlled by a mass flow controller (MFC, Alicat Scientific MC). Both the catholyte and anolyte were a stream of 1 M KOH electrolyte, and the flow rates were both controlled to be 0.5 ml min-1 by a peristaltic pump (Harvard apparatus, P70-7000). A wide cell voltage ranging from 2.0 V to 8.0 V was controlled by a potentialstat (EnergyLab XM, Solartron Analytical), while the cathode potential was simultaneously measured by the auxiliary channel of EnergyLab XM in reference to an Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl, CHI111) reference electrode. Since the CO2 consumption rate including CO2 electrolysis and chemical neutralization rate is high at the flow cell, the CO2 cannot be used as the reference gas. Thus, the gas from the outlet of the flow cell was mixed with an argon stream with a fixed flow rate of 10 sccm before looping to the gas chromatography (GC, Agilent 7890B) for quantification of the gas products. The gas sample was injected to the GC at 5 min of electrolysis. The GC was calibrated by three independent calibration gas cylinders, which contain five different components (CO, CH4, C2H4, C2H6 and H2) with a concentration of 1000, 5000, and 10000 ppm, respectively. The liquid products were collected at the outlet of buffer layer, and then identified and quantified by 1H nuclear magnetic resolution (NMR, Bruker AV500) analysis.

sections.heading: 2.5 CO2 electro-reduction on Cu/Pt/ZnO tandem electrodes.
sections.text: The distance between flow cell and GC connected by a PTFE tube with 1/8-inch outer diameter was reduced to less than 15.0 cm for instant analysis. The testing method was the same as the regular CO2 electro-reduction testing except the sample gas was injected at the 1 min of the electrolysis. A cathode potential of -0.71 V vs. RHE was applied constantly through this testing.

sections.heading: 2.6 Characterization.
sections.text: The CO electro-oxidation was characterized by cyclic voltammetry (CV) right after the CO2 electro-reduction reaction. The CV was conducted in a three-electrode system, using 1 M KOH as electrolyte. A scan rate of 5 mV s-1 was set to scan the electrode from 0.5 to 1.0 V vs. RHE. The sample for cross-sectional image was prepared by cutting the electrode using a scalpel, and imaged by scanning electron microscopy (FEI, SCIOS DualBeam).

sections.heading: 3.1 Characterization of Cu/ZnO tandem electrodes.
sections.text:
The PFR is more efficient than the CSTR regarding the conversion of CO feedstock in the CO-CO coupling reaction to form C2+ products with a positive reaction order n > 0 for CO (Figure S1-2). That is because CO concentration through the volume of the PFR decreases gradually instead of an abrupt drop of CO concentration to the lower value in the CSTR (Figure 1a). Inspired by the higher efficiency of PFR, we designed a two-layer tandem gas diffusion electrode (GDE) with a spatial arrangement of ZnO catalyst layer on top of the Cu catalyst layer, which intends to mimic the CO conversion along the catalyst layer from the catalyst layer/electrolyte interface to the catalyst layer/gas diffusion layer interface to that in the PFR (Figure 1a and 1b). Figure 1c shows the cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image of a representative Cu/ZnO tandem electrode with the Cu and ZnO loadings of 1.0 and 0.20 mg cm-2, respectively. The corresponding energy-dispersive Xray spectroscopy (EDX) elemental mapping clearly shows the layer-by-layer structure consisting of the ZnO catalyst layer on top of the Cu catalyst layer (Figure 1d). In such a Cu/ZnO tandem electrode when incorporated in a flow cell (Figure S3), the CO2-to-CO reduction occurs in the ZnO catalyst layer, and the generated supplementary CO molecules
6 are progressively converted to C2+ products in the Cu catalyst layer via reductive coupling reaction as they transport backwardly along the Cu catalyst layer (Figure 1b). As a comparison, we also prepared a Cu&ZnO mixed electrode whose one-layer catalyst layer is composed of Cu and ZnO nanoparticles mixed physically and randomly (Figure 1f, g, and h). The Cu&ZnO mixed electrode has the same loading of respective Cu and ZnO as that in the Cu/ZnO tandem electrode. The temporal and spatial profiles of CO concentration in the Cu&ZnO mixed electrode are analogous to those in the CSTR (Figure 1a, e, and f).
7
8

sections.heading: 3.2 CO2 electro-reduction in the flow cell.
sections.text:
The Cu&ZnO mixed electrode shows improved production rates of both the C2H4 and C2+ products compared to the bare Cu electrode. However, the FE for C2+ products decreases at a representative potential of -0.72 ± 0.10 V (vs. RHE thereafter), as shown in Figure 2a, b and Figure S4-6. In the meanwhile, an obvious increase of both the FE of CO and jCO was observed for the Cu&ZnO mixed electrode, which indicates an insufficient CO utilization. Instead, the two-layer Cu/ZnO tandem electrode exhibits much higher FE and production rate for C2+ products than those for both Cu&ZnO mixed electrode and bare Cu electrode. Specifically, the FE of C2+ products over the Cu/ZnO tandem electrode are increased by 1.2 and 1.3 times respectively, compared to the bare Cu and Cu&ZnO mixed electrode at -0.72 ± 0.10 V, while the partial current density of C2+ products (jC2+) is increased by 3.4 and 1.8 times, respectively (Figure 2b and Figure S6). C2H4 is the predominant C2+ products. The Cu/ZnO tandem electrode also shows FE of C2H4 and jC2H4 1.3 and 1.8 times higher than those for the Cu&ZnO mixed electrode, respectively. In contrast, both the FE and the production rate of CO for the Cu/ZnO tandem electrode are reduced compared to the Cu&ZnO mixed electrode, while its FE of CO is even lower than that of the bare Cu electrode. It is worth pointing out that the CO formation dominated potential range for ZnO should be largely overlapped with the C2+ products generation dominated potential range for Cu to allow for the synergistic function between the two catalyst layers in the tandem electrodes. The commercial Cu and ZnO nanoparticles meet this requirement according to their respective activity and selectivity towards C2+ products and CO (Figure S7 and S8). Theoretically, the C-C coupling reaction on the Cu surface is not an energy-intensive step based on the density functional theory calculation assuming the *CO surface coverage is high enough.[2, 24-26] The previous CO electro-reduction on Cu electrodes showed an onset potential of around -0.3 V to initiate the C2+ formation with FE 37.2-68.7%, which is quite consistent with the theoretical overpotential value.[25, 27, 28] However, in the case of CO2 electro-reduction on the Cu electrode, the acceleration of the C2+ products generation rate starts at a more cathodic potential of -0.55 V, and the onset FE of C2+ (< 13.3%) is much lower (Figure 2c and 2d). The gap between the theoretical and experimental onset potentials for C2+ products formation from CO2 electro-reduction is caused by the low *CO surface coverage on the Cu surface at the low overpotential region. The ZnO catalyst or catalyst layer provides supplementary CO in addition to the CO generated by Cu catalyst itself to increase the local concentration of CO nearby the Cu sites, leading to the enhancement of the production rate of C2+ products. However, the FE of C2+ products is determined by the extent of CO utilization for C-C coupling under different local CO concentrations. The balance of CO2-to-CO reaction rate for ZnO and CO-to-C2+ products reaction rate for Cu, which is determined by the intrinsic activity and loading of each catalyst, plays a key role in achieving the maximum FE of C2+ products in the tandem electrodes. To evaluate this effect, five Cu/ZnO tandem electrodes were fabricated, which possess the same Cu loading of 1.0 mg cm-2 but varying ZnO loading from 0.05 to 0.3 mg cm-2. Their performances were tested under identical conditions. The detailed product distribution and total current density of each
9 electrode are shown in Figure S9. The onset potential of C2+ products formation shifts anodically as the ZnO loading gradually increases (Figure 2c and 2d). When the ZnO content is increased to 0.3 mg cm-2, the overpotential is reduced by ~0.5 V compared with the bare Cu electrode. That is because the feeding of supplementary CO facilitates the reaction kinetics of CO-to-C2+ products reaction. The achievable maximum FE of C2+ products also steadily increases as the ZnO content increases up to 0.2 mg cm-2 (Figure 2c). Further increasing the ZnO loading results in a drop of the FE of C2+ products at high overpotentials because the supplementary CO feeding rate by ZnO exceeds the CO consumption rate by Cu. The optimal Cu1.0/ZnO0.20 tandem electrode, involving loading of Cu 1.0 mg cm-2 and ZnO 0.20 mg cm2, reaches a maximum FE of 78% for C2+ products at -0.73 V, under which the jC2+ is -466 mA cm-2. Among all the C2+ products, C2H4 is the predominant product followed by ethanol (C2H5OH). The FE of C2H4 and jC2H4 as a function of ZnO loading shows a similar trend as those for C2+ products. The Cu1.0/ZnO0.20 tandem electrode shows a 49% FE of C2H4 at -0.73 V, under which jC2H4 reaches -292 mA cm-2 (Figure S6 and S10). The production rate of CH4 and C2+ liquid products are also improved as the loading of ZnO increases (Figure S11). However, the trend of how the FE of C2+ oxygenates changes along with the increase of ZnO loading is elusive. That’s because the commercial Cu nanoparticles favor the C2 gas product of C2H4 over C2+ liquid products.The Cu/ZnO tandem electrodes beat all Cu-Zn bimetallic catalysts in overall performance in terms of the activity and selectivity toward C2+ products formation (Figure 2e).

sections.heading: 3.3 The utilization efficiency of CO intermediate.
sections.text:
To further unravel the underlying mechanism of the potential and mass loading dependent behavior of FE of C2+ products, we analyzed the CO utilization efficiency, which is specifically referred to the ratio of CO dimerization rate over the CO generation rate (DCO/GCO). The CO dimerization rate is normalized from the production rates of C2+ products (see calculation details in the exiperimental section) since they are derived from the *CO intermediate. The CO generation rate is referred to as the summary of the production rates of dimerized CO, CO reduced to form C1 hydrocarbon, and CO gas product (Figure S12). The DCO/GCO ratios for three typical applied potentials are demonstrated in Figure 2f. The DCO/GCO depends on the interplay of the Cu/ZnO mass ratio and the applied potential. The values of DCO/GCO for all Cu/ZnO tandem electrodes are increased compared with the bare Cu electrode. At a relatively low potential of -0.62 V, the DCO/GCO is monotonously increased with the increasing of ZnO mass loading in the tandem electrodes. However, as the potential negatively increases to -0.70 V and beyond, a peak value of DCO/GCO was observed at a ZnO mass loading of 0.2 mg cm-2. That means the CO dimerization rate is growing much faster than the CO supply rate until reaching a threshold value of the CO supply rate. The ZnO catalyst layer provides supplementary CO to increase the local CO concentration on the Cu surface and in turn, *CO surface coverage, leading to the acceleration of CO-to-C2+ products conversion. An optimal ZnO mass loading for a specific potential supplies CO in a rate that achieves a saturation of *CO surface coverage. Further increasing of ZnO mass loading results in an excess supply of CO, and subsequently lowers the DCO/GCO as in the cases of ZnO mass loading of 0.30 mg cm-2 at -0.70 and -0.73 V. Besides, the optimal ZnO mass loading is also sensitive to the applied potential. That is because the overpotential governs both CO supply rates on Cu and ZnO
10
catalysts and CO dimerization rate on the Cu catalyst. Note that the balance between CO supply rate and CO dimerization rate can only determine the optimum FE of C2+ products, while the selectivity toward one specific multi-carbon product, such as C2H4 and C2H5OH, is also affected by the CO concentration.[14, 25]

sections.heading: 3.4 Proof of CO back-diffusion through catalyst layer.
3.5 Stability of the Cu/ZnO tandem electrode.
sections.text:
For a practical electrode, the stability is important as much, if not more, as the activity. The stability of the Cu/ZnO tandem electrode was evaluated under a very high total current density of -600 mA cm-2 (Figure 4). The FE of C2H4 was 50% in the first two hours and still
12
maintained 80% of its initial value after ten-hour continuous running. The FE of C2H5OH kept at around 20% during the 10-hour test. Further increase of the stability needs better water management in the electrode.
Figure 4. Stability of the Cu1.0/Zn0.20 tandem electrode under 10-hour continuous operation at a high current density of -600 mA cm-2 in a flow cell with 1 M KOH electrolyte.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
The layer-by-layer tandem electrode was designed for CO2-to-C2+ products conversion with a high FE and production rate based on the concept of PFR using CO as the intermediate feedstock. By simply adjusting the mass ratio of Cu over ZnO, the Cu/ZnO tandem electrodes can be flexibly optimized to reach a compromise between activity and selectivity towards C2+ products. The optimal Cu1.0/ZnO0.20 tandem electrode exhibits 3.4 and 1.8 times increase in production rate for C2+ products at -0.72 V vs. RHE compared to the bare Cu and CSTR analogous Cu&ZnO mixed electrodes, respectively, while the FE of C2+ products is enhanced by 1.2 and 1.3 times, respectively. Our design strategy of the tandem electrode can be applied to any couple of C2+- and CO-selective catalysts to improve the yield of overall C2+ products or a specific C2+ product depending on the selectivity of the used catalyst.
